'''Paul M. Cook''' (April 25, 1924<ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Paul M. Cook |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/cook-paul-m|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name="oral">{{cite book|first=  James J. |last=Bohning|title=Paul M. Cook, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by James J. Bohning at San Carlos, California on 2 April 1992 |date=2 April 1992 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/cook_pm_0105_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref> – December 14, 2020) was an American businessman who was the founder and CEO of [[Raychem]], a chemical manufacturing company that reached $2&nbsp;billion in annual revenue. In 1988, he was awarded the [[National Medal of Technology and Innovation|National Medal of Technology]] "[f]or his vision and entrepreneurial efforts, his technical accomplishments and his business and technical leadership as the key contributor in creating a worldwide chemically based industry."

==Early life and education==
Paul Cook took an early interest in chemistry, and developed a chemistry lab in the basement of his parents' home.<ref name="oral"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/radiationchemistry.html |title=Commercialization of Radiation Chemistry |publisher=[[American Chemical Society]] |date=April 9, 1997 |access-date=August 21, 2015}}</ref> After he graduated high school in 1941, he started at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), studying chemical engineering under [[Warren K. Lewis]].<ref name="oral"/>

In 1943, Cook enlisted in the United States Army and enrolled in the Army Specialized Training Program; through that program, he attended [[Stanford University]] for two terms, studying mechanical engineering. Cook was then sent to Hunter Liggett Military Reservation and then [[Fort Benning]], where he completed Officer Candidate School. He was then sent to fight in Italy. Cook served in combat with the [[10th Mountain Division]].<ref name="oral"/>

In 1946, Cook left the army and worked for [[Submarine signals|Submarine Signal]] in Boston. He then returned to MIT and completed his Bachelor of Science in 1947.<ref name="hoot"/><ref name="oral"/>

==Career==
Cook was one of [[SRI International]]'s earliest employees, joining the organization in 1948 as its 48th employee.<ref name="bhof"/> He went on to lead SRI's [[Radiochemistry|Radiation Chemistry]] Laboratory, where he was interested in using high-energy electrons to alter polymers.<ref name="hoot"/>

In 1951, Cook founded the [[Sequoia Process Corporation]]; he left that after five years to found [[Raychem]], which opened in 1957, and focused on commercial applications for radiochemistry.<ref name="oral"/> He served as Raychem's CEO and chairman of the board.<ref name="hoot"/>

Cook founded other companies, including [[CellNet Data Systems]], [[DIVA Systems]] (1995), and [[Promptu]].<ref name="hoot"/><ref>{{cite news|url=https://hbr.org/1990/03/the-business-of-innovation-an-interview-with-paul-cook|title=The Business of Innovation: An Interview with Paul Cook|work=Harvard Business Review|date=March–April 1990|access-date=2015-08-21}}</ref>

==Awards and memberships==
Cook served on SRI International's board of directors for nine years and served as its chairman for six of those.<ref name="hoot"/>

In 1986, he was awarded the [[Winthrop-Sears Medal]] from the Chemical Industry Association.<ref name="bhof"/> In 1988, [[Ronald Reagan]] awarded him the [[National Medal of Technology and Innovation|National Medal of Technology]].<ref name="bhof"/><ref name="reag"/>

He received the [[Bay Area Council]]'s Bay Area Business Hall of Fame Award in 1999,<ref name="bhof"/> and SRI's Weldon B. "Hoot" Gibson Achievement Award in 2008.<ref name="hoot"/>
